readnow.text: No new chapter today. Keep your book close so you can look back at the whole novel.

warmup.text: Read Eldorado again, slowly. On Day 2 you saw two parts of the poem work together. Today put all of them together and say what the poem means about searching for gold.

words.text: Explain a root in your own words, pick an option on the vocabulary choice board, and explain one editing rule. Then proofread Jack's last letter, to an old friend in the diggings.

reading.text: Look back over the whole novel: the voyage, the diggings, and the ending. Answer the pause questions and the three synthesis questions. Use moments from the beginning, the middle, and the end.

assignment.text: This is it. Read your whole story out loud one last time, ending and all. Put the final version in the box with its title. Then copy your work into Canvas.

game.title: Jack's Letter to the Diggings
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 lines today
game.look: This letter is made up for the game, the way Jack writes letters home in Chapters 2 and 3. Every line has one misspelled word. Tap it, then tap the right spelling to ink the line clean. A clean letter gets a wax seal.

do: Read the line of the letter.
Tap the word that is spelled wrong.
Tap the right spelling to ink it clean.
how.why: Proofreading means checking every word on purpose, the way an editor does before a piece is published.

game.doneLine: Four letters, twenty-four lines, every one clean.

lines.text: You will never [gess] what happened in San Francisco Bay.
lines.why: guess has a silent u after the g.
lines.miss: There is a silent letter after the g.

lines.text: The riverboat's boiler [exploaded], and our gold sank to the bottom.
lines.why: explode drops its e before -ed: exploded.

lines.text: Praiseworthy said it was only bits of [coloured] metal, and he meant it.
lines.why: American spelling is colored. Coloured is the British way.
lines.miss: This is an American book. Use the American spelling.

lines.text: Every storekeeper in the [audiance] wanted a cat for a ratter.
lines.why: aud means hear. audience: the people who hear, ending in -ence.
lines.miss: Find the root aud, then the ending -ence.

lines.text: Aunt Arabella and my sisters [arived] on a ship the very same day!
We are building a cabin, and you are [invitted].
lines.why: invite drops its e before -ed: invited. One t.
lines.miss: invite + ed: one t, and one e drops.

virtue.name: hope
virtue.title: The most hopeful moment this week
virtue.intro: Look back at Chapters 16 to 18. Tap the moment you think shows hope the most.

options.t: The whole trip looks like a wild-goose chase to Jack, but the partners keep digging on the hill (Chapter 16).
Praiseworthy on the morning of the fight: “Not on your life, Jack. We'll make it.” (Chapter 17).
After the gold sinks: “Mere bits of colored metal” (Chapter 18).
Jack, soaking wet and penniless: “Maybe he'll let us work our passage back” (Chapter 18).

art.title: View of San Francisco in 1850
art.alt: An oil painting of a young town of wooden buildings on sandy hills, with the bay and far hills behind and a few people and horses on a dirt road.
art.look: George Henry Burgess lived in San Francisco during the Gold Rush. In 1878 he painted the city as it looked in 1850, when it had grown from a small town almost overnight. This is the place where the novel begins and ends.
